chapter.name: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability
chapter.blurb: Random events and the probability scale, experimental and theoretical probability, sample spaces and events, tree diagrams and the long-run behaviour of chance.

scope_in.item: Random experiments and events; the probability scale 0 to 1 and words like impossible and certain
Experimental probability as relative frequency; sample versus population
Theoretical probability with equally likely outcomes
Sample space, sample size and events as subsets
Tree diagrams for multi-step experiments and simple probabilities from them
Law of Large Numbers, independence, Gambler's fallacy, fair and unbiased

concepts.name: Randomness and the probability scale
concepts.description: Random experiments and events, subjective probability, and measuring likelihood on a scale from 0 to 1.
concepts.idea: A random experiment has known possible outcomes but an unpredictable result; probability measures how likely an event is.
concepts.rule: Probability lies between 0 and 1: 0 is impossible, 1 is certain, 0.5 is an even chance. 0 <= P(E) <= 1.
concepts.example: A probability of 0.75 for winning a match means a 75% chance, so winning is more likely than not.

questions.q: Explain what subjective probability means, with an example.
questions.a: It is a person's own estimate of how likely an event is, based on their reading of the evidence. For example, one friend says it is unlikely to rain because the sun is bright while another says it may rain because it is hot.
s: It is a personal estimate based on the evidence they see
Gives an example such as the rain prediction

questions.q: Why is rain regarded as a random event, and how can we still speak about its probability?
questions.a: Rain depends on many complex factors such as temperature, humidity, wind and pressure, and is so sensitive to them that we cannot predict it with certainty. But from data about past patterns we can estimate how likely rain is, i.e. its probability.
s: Rain depends on many sensitive factors
It cannot be predicted with certainty
Probability can still be estimated from data on patterns

questions.q: Ravi says an event with probability 1.5 is very likely. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Probabilities lie between 0 and 1, so 1.5 is not a possible probability.

questions.q: Give one example each of an impossible event, an event with even chance and a certain event, for a die roll or a coin toss, with their probabilities.
questions.a: Rolling a 9 on a die: probability 0. Getting heads on a fair coin: 1/2. Rolling a number from 1 to 6 on a die: 1.

concepts.name: Experimental probability and relative frequency
concepts.description: Estimating probability from experiments or data as a relative frequency, and using a sample to estimate for a population.
concepts.idea: When outcomes are not known to be equally likely, we estimate probability from how often an event occurs in trials.
concepts.rule: Experimental probability = (number of times the event occurred)/(total number of trials), also called the relative frequency. A larger, representative sample gives a more reliable estimate for the population.
concepts.example: A die rolled 50 times lands on 4 eight times: experimental probability 8/50 = 0.16.

questions.q: A die rolled 12 times gives a 3 three times. Why might this differ from 1/6, and what happens with 60, 600 or 6000 rolls?
questions.a: With only 12 trials chance variation can be large, so 3/12 differs from 1/6. As the number of trials grows the relative frequency tends to get closer to 1/6.

questions.a: Frequency 15; relative frequency 15/50 = 0.3. Estimate: 0.3 x 1200 = 360 students.

questions.q: Nita says a sample of just 3 students is enough to predict the favourite fruit of the whole school. Evaluate.

questions.q: Plan a survey to estimate the probability that a student in your school walks to school. Say the sample size, how you make it representative and how you compute the estimate.
questions.a: Ask, say, 100 students chosen from different classes and grades. Count the number who walk. The estimate is (number who walk)/100, and it can be used to predict for the whole school.
s: Sample drawn from different classes so it is representative
Estimate = number who walk / sample size

concepts.name: Theoretical probability with equally likely outcomes
concepts.description: Probability as the number of favourable outcomes divided by the number of possible equally likely outcomes.
concepts.idea: When every outcome is equally likely we can find a probability by counting, without any experiment.
concepts.rule: P(A) = (number of favourable outcomes)/(number of possible outcomes), when all outcomes are equally likely.
concepts.example: A letter picked at random from PROBABILITY is B with probability 2/11.

questions.q: Theoretical probability of an event is

concepts.name: Sample spaces and events
concepts.description: Listing the sample space of an experiment, its sample size, and events as subsets of the sample space.
concepts.idea: The sample space lists every possible outcome exactly once, and an event is a chosen group of these outcomes.
concepts.rule: The sample space S must include every outcome once; n(S) is the sample size. An event is a subset of S.
concepts.example: Tossing two coins: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}; the event at least one head is {HH, HT, TH}.

concepts.name: Tree diagrams and multi-step experiments
concepts.description: Using tree diagrams to list all outcomes of experiments with several steps and to find probabilities.
concepts.idea: A tree diagram shows every path of a multi-step experiment, and each path is one outcome.
concepts.rule: Draw a branch for every outcome of each step; each complete path is an outcome. Count favourable paths over all paths when they are equally likely, or multiply probabilities along a path.
concepts.example: Two fair coins: the tree has 4 paths, so P(HH) = 1/4 and P(one head and one tail) = 2/4 = 1/2.

questions.q: A tree diagram is used to
questions.a: list all possible outcomes of a multi-step experiment

A student guesses all 3 questions of a test with 4 options each. Find the probability of exactly 2 correct answers.
questions.a: There are 3 ways to choose which two are correct. Each such way has probability (1/4) x (1/4) x (3/4) = 3/64. Total 3 x 3/64 = 9/64.
s: 3 ways to pick the two correct questions

questions.q: Two dice are rolled. Find the probability that the sum is a prime number greater than 5.
questions.a: Prime sums greater than 5 are 7 and 11. A sum of 7 occurs in 6 ways and a sum of 11 in 2 ways, out of 36. P = 8/36 = 2/9.

questions.q: Sam says that for two coin tosses P(two heads) = 1/3 because the outcomes are "no head", "one head", "two heads". Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Those three outcomes are not equally likely. The tree shows 4 equally likely outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT, so P(two heads) = 1/4.
s: Says the three outcomes are not equally likely

questions.q: Describe the tree diagram for tossing a coin and then rolling a die. How many paths does it have and what is the probability of heads and a 6?
questions.a: The first stage has 2 branches (H, T). From each branch there are 6 branches for the die. So there are 12 paths and P(heads and 6) = 1/12.
s: Two branches then six from each

concepts.name: Long-run behaviour, the Gambler's fallacy and fair experiments
concepts.description: The Law of Large Numbers, independence of trials, the Gambler's fallacy and what fair and unbiased mean.
concepts.idea: Probability describes what happens in the long run; it does not say what the next trial will be, and a fair coin has no memory.
concepts.rule: As the number of trials increases the experimental probability tends to the theoretical probability (Law of Large Numbers). Trials are independent: past results do not change the next probability. The Gambler's fallacy is thinking they do.
concepts.example: After six heads in a row, a fair coin still has probability 1/2 of tails on the next toss.

questions.q: The Law of Large Numbers says that as the number of trials increases,
questions.a: experimental probability tends to get closer to theoretical probability
o: experimental probability tends to get closer to theoretical probability

questions.a: after a run of one outcome the opposite outcome becomes more likely
o: after a run of one outcome the opposite outcome becomes more likely

questions.q: In Snakes and Ladders Asha has rolled 6 three times in a row and says she cannot get another 6. Explain her mistake.
questions.a: This is the Gambler's fallacy. Each roll of a fair die is independent, so the probability of a 6 is still 1/6 on the next roll.

questions.q: A fair coin is tossed 100 times. What relative frequency of heads do you expect, and will it be exactly this?
questions.a: Close to 0.5. It need not be exactly 0.5 because chance causes small variations.

questions.q: A die is rolled 12 times and shows a 3 three times. Give the experimental and theoretical probabilities of a 3 and the number of 3s you would expect in 6000 rolls.
questions.a: Experimental 3/12 = 1/4; theoretical 1/6. In 6000 rolls expect about 6000 x 1/6 = 1000 threes.

questions.q: Explain the statement "probability does not tell you what will happen next but what will happen in the long run".
questions.a: For one trial the outcome is unpredictable. But over very many trials the relative frequency settles near the theoretical probability, as in the Law of Large Numbers.

questions.q: A friend tosses a coin 5 times and gets 5 heads, and says the coin must be biased. Evaluate.
questions.a: For a fair coin the probability of 5 heads in 5 tosses is (1/2)^5 = 1/32, which is small but not impossible. With so few trials this is weak evidence. He should toss it many more times before concluding.
s: P(5 heads) = 1/32 for a fair coin
Says 5 tosses is too few to decide

questions.q: Vik says that after six heads in a row tails is "due" and is now more likely. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. This is the Gambler's fallacy. The coin has no memory, so tails still has probability 1/2.
s: States it is the Gambler's fallacy

questions.q: Design an experiment to check whether a coin is fair.
questions.a: Toss the coin a large number of times, say 500, and record the heads. Compute the relative frequency of heads. If it stays close to 0.5 as the number of tosses grows, the coin looks fair. If it stays far from 0.5, it may be biased.
s: Toss many times and record results
Compute the relative frequency of heads
Compare with 0.5 as the trials increase
